findings.title: NEW - the fix that closed F-16 made a non-vacuity claim false in three step test descriptions
findings.detail: The plan verifier's item W09 asked each check_access_model.py step test to prove it was not a discovery no-op, and steps[M2-S01].acceptance_tests[1], steps[M2-S02].acceptance_tests[2] and steps[M2-S03].acceptance_tests[0] all answer it the same way: 'against an empty directory this checker exits 1 ... so it is not a discovery no-op'. Measured this run, an empty --manifest-dir produces a WARN ('no profile, permission set, or permission set group metadata files found') with "blocking": 0 and exits 0. None of the three declared commands passes --strict, so as declared all three would now pass against an empty step directory, and so would M2-T1. The build is not currently exposed: check-outputs must confirm every declared outputs[] path exists and is non-empty before set-status built is allowed, the always-on manifest test fails a metadata step with no package.xml, and a missing --manifest-dir is now a usage error exiting 1. What is broken is the claim - W09's answer no longer follows from the checker's behaviour. This is F-16's pattern inverted: a rule added under a finished step turned green to red, and an exit policy narrowed under three finished steps turned a stated guarantee into an unstated one. Both times the step tests were not re-run.

process_observations.observation: The F-16 remedy landed at the right layer. It could have been closed by trimming one description on one step, and was instead closed by fixing the exit policy that let a length advisory fail a milestone - which also closed F-17, the finding that said the three checkers should decide this once rather than per plan.

The fix protected the assertion it narrowed. Raising check 2 (migratable permissions still on a profile) from WARN to HIGH in the same commit is the easy part to skip and the expensive part to miss: without it, 'no migratable permission left on a profile' - half of M2-T1's declared assertion - would have become a non-blocking advisory and the test would have passed a profile carrying objectPermissions. Negative control C injected exactly that and got exit 1 with blocking 1.

The merged manifest was recomputed from the five step manifests and correctly left alone: member sets identical, byte-identical to the canonical render, mtime untouched. On the M1 side, a manifest whose content and mtime drifted apart is F-18, so not rewriting an unchanged file keeps its mtime an honest record of when its content was last decided.

Every file-checkable half of the six tester-deferred manual lines was re-run against the artefacts rather than copied forward, and all six still hold - zero <users> elements across the six queue and group files, exactly one sharingCriteriaRules block, Private on Case.object-meta.xml line 5, no settings-meta.xml anywhere, four top-level children on the integration permission set, and the runbook's three skew criteria. That is what makes the checklist narrower for the human rather than just longer.

A skill fix moved a claim from true to false under three finished steps. F-16 was a rule added under a finished step (green to red); F-22 is an exit policy narrowed under three (a stated guarantee to an unstated one). Two instances in six days, in opposite directions, from two commits to the same skill - and both times nothing in the loop re-ran the affected step tests while the plan's prose kept asserting the older behaviour.

A deferred manual test never reached the gate's checklist. tests/M2-S04/results.json has four skipped_manual[] entries and v1's checklist carried three, with its own prose saying five where six were deferred. Step 7 is a gather-all step with no count assertion behind it, so an omission is silent - nothing would have caught this one if the re-verification had not re-walked the results files.

No agent in the loop may correct a stale test description, and there are now five. amend-step is refused on a documented step (pending or blocked only), so each waits on a v6 re-plan or on a rebuild of the step it sits on. Four consecutive verification runs have recorded prose that no agent is permitted to fix, and the list grows one entry per run.

The 200-character description headroom is enforced on exactly the metadata types that were already compliant. Region__c at 249 characters and Bypass_Case_Intake_Validation at 250 are within six characters of the 255-character platform limit that broke mock deploy run 1, and no checker in the library reads a CustomField or CustomPermission description at all. The rule went where the failure was observed rather than where it can recur.

Whether F-16's remedy is complete is a human call. 'Advisories should not fail a milestone' is done. 'Descriptions should have headroom' is not - the description is still 244 characters, M2-S01 was never rebuilt, and its step-level test result is five days and two checker versions old. The two intents were never separated, so closing one reads as closing both.

Whether F-20's backwards position counts as an ordering contradiction in the Step 9 sense decides between ready-with-findings and not-ready. This report reads it as a finding the human may accept, consistently with v1, which attributed its not-ready verdict to F-16 alone - so removing F-16 removes the verdict. A human who weighs F-20 differently should reject the gate, and the finding is in front of them either way.

Whether Case_Tier1/Case_Tier2 and the two Tier profiles should collapse is unresolved. Both pairs are byte-identical apart from label and description, re-diffed this run, and no answered clarification distinguishes Tier 2's access from Tier 1's - the requirement's split is routing and escalation, neither of which is access. It depends on whether the two teams are expected to diverge on access later.

The SharingRules container versus SharingCriteriaRule rule-type manifest form is unsettled. The cited skill's metadata-examples.md section 6 prescribes the rule-type form and says SharingRules is not what you address; two other skills in the library manifest the container form; the step chose the container form so the manifest test's file-stem derivation would cover the file; and all three mock-deploy runs were source-mode, so no deploy has read either form for this file.

Tier 2's queue mailbox is a posture with no address: Q88 answers 'a shared mailbox' and names no address anywhere on file, metadata-builder will not invent one, and check_queues.py confirms Tier_2_Engineering carries no <email> at all. The artefact is right and the test criterion is not, and only a human can say which should change. This is the one checklist line whose evidence is a mismatch, and it must not be ticked as written.

The merged manifest is worth risk-scoring against the target org before the human runs the optional validate-only command, because 19 members across Profile, PermissionSet and SharingRules is the change class where an org's existing state matters most.

billing_visibility_reconciliation.asymmetry: Tier 1's exclusion is proved by finding NO file; Billing's own access is proved by finding a queue in a DIFFERENT step, and it does not work until M3-S04 (pending) transfers ownership to that queue. A reviewer reading only M2-S05 would not learn where Billing's access comes from.
billing_visibility_reconciliation.what_an_artefact_now_reconciles: artefacts/M2-S05/case-visibility-model.md section 'How each team actually reaches a case' states all three rows and names queue ownership explicitly: 'This is queue ownership, not a sharing rule. No sharing rule was written for Billing, because A1's conservative reading is about keeping others out, and the Billing team's own access already exists through the queue.' Both halves of its one-sentence denial statement were re-verified on disk this run - Case.object-meta.xml line 5 carries Private, and the sharing rule mentions Billing only inside a <description>.
billing_visibility_reconciliation.what_is_still_open: Nothing in plan.json records the composition. A1.steps[] names M2-S05 alone, and no decision entry ties M2-S04's queue to M2-S05's absence as two halves of one answer.
billing_visibility_reconciliation.consequence: A later change to M2-S04's queue - a second Billing queue, or dropping queue-based ownership for direct assignment - could silently break Billing's access to its own cases without touching anything M2-S05 owns, and nothing in the build would flag the connection.
billing_visibility_reconciliation.what_the_gate_should_do: Accept, in the same breath as manual checklist line 1, that Billing visibility = queue ownership (M2-S04) + no competing restriction (M2-S05's deliberate absence), and ask for that composition to be recorded at plan level rather than only in one step's documentation artefact.
